content: Uterine fibroids, also called leiomyomas or myomas, are benign (non-cancerous) tumors composed of smooth muscle cells and fibrous connective tissue that develop within the muscular wall of the uterus. These growths are common in women of reproductive age, especially between ages 30 and 50, and vary widely in size, number, and location. The exact cause of fibroids remains unclear, but their growth is believed to be influenced by estrogen and progesterone hormones. Fibroids can be asymptomatic or cause symptoms including heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pain or pressure, bladder or bowel dysfunction, and reproductive issues such as infertility or pregnancy complications. Diagnosis typically involves pelvic examination and imaging studies like ultrasound or MRI. Risk factors include age, African American ethnicity, family history, obesity, and early onset of menstruation. Management depends on the severity of symptoms and reproductive goals and may range from watchful waiting to medical treatments like hormonal therapy or minimally invasive procedures such as uterine artery embolization or focused ultrasound. Surgery, including myomectomy or hysterectomy, may be required in some cases. While fibroids are benign, their location and size may impact quality of life. Safety considerations include side effects of therapies, risks of surgery, and potential impacts on fertility and pregnancy. Limitations of current knowledge include incomplete understanding of fibroid pathogenesis and variability in treatment outcomes. This module aims to provide clear, evidence-based education covering causes, symptoms, diagnosis, management options, misconceptions, and safety considerations to support informed decisions and improved health outcomes.

chunk_title: Definition and Types of Uterine Fibroids
content: Uterine fibroids, medically referred to as leiomyomas or myomas, are benign tumors arising from the smooth muscle layer (myometrium) of the uterus. They vary in size from microscopic nodules to large masses that can distort the uterine shape. Fibroids are classified based on their location in the uterus: submucosal (beneath the uterine lining), intramural (within the muscular wall), and subserosal (on the outer uterine surface). Each type may result in different symptoms and clinical implications.

chunk_title: Causes and Mechanisms of Fibroid Development
content: The exact cause of uterine fibroids is not fully understood, but their growth is influenced by hormonal factors, especially estrogen and progesterone. These hormones promote the proliferation of smooth muscle cells in the uterus. Genetic factors also play a role; fibroids often run in families. Molecular studies suggest mutations in specific genes and alterations in growth factors contribute to clonal expansion of fibroid cells. Inflammatory processes and extracellular matrix changes also support fibroid development.

content: Uterine fibroids are very common, affecting up to 70-80% of women by age 50. African American women have a higher incidence and tend to develop fibroids at a younger age with more severe symptoms. Other risk factors include early menarche (early start of menstruation), obesity, family history, nulliparity (never given birth), and higher blood pressure. Protective factors may include use of hormonal contraception and having multiple pregnancies.

content: Many women with fibroids are asymptomatic and discover them incidentally. When symptoms occur, they commonly include heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia), pelvic pain or pressure, frequent urination due to bladder compression, constipation from bowel pressure, and lower back pain. Submucosal fibroids may cause infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss. Severe anemia may result from chronic heavy bleeding.

content: Diagnosis typically begins with a pelvic exam where an enlarged or irregular uterus may be palpated. Imaging is essential; transvaginal ultrasound is the first-line modality due to accessibility and non-invasiveness. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides detailed anatomy and helps in surgical planning. Other methods such as hysteroscopy or saline infusion sonography can evaluate submucosal fibroids affecting the uterine cavity.

chunk_title: Impact of Fibroids on Fertility and Pregnancy
content: Fibroids, particularly submucosal and large intramural types, can interfere with fertility by disrupting the uterine lining or blocking fallopian tubes. During pregnancy, fibroids may increase risks of miscarriage, preterm labor, abnormal fetal position, and postpartum hemorrhage. However, many women with fibroids have normal pregnancies. The size, location, and number of fibroids influence the degree of risk.

content: Medical treatments aim to control symptoms and reduce fibroid size. Options include hormonal therapies such as gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists, which induce a temporary menopausal state, reducing fibroid volume. Oral contraceptives and progestins may help regulate bleeding but do not shrink fibroids. Emerging treatments like selective progesterone receptor modulators (SPRMs) show promise. Non-hormonal options focus on symptom relief, such as NSAIDs for pain.

content: Minimally invasive options include uterine artery embolization (UAE), which reduces fibroid blood supply causing shrinkage, and MRI-guided focused ultrasound that destroys fibroid tissue using thermal energy. Surgical approaches include myomectomy, removal of fibroids preserving the uterus, and hysterectomy, complete removal of the uterus. The choice depends on symptom severity, fibroid characteristics, and desire for future fertility.

content: While many treatments improve symptoms, none guarantee prevention of fibroid recurrence. Medical therapies may have side effects such as menopausal symptoms with GnRH agonists. Surgical procedures carry usual operative risks including bleeding and infection and potential impacts on fertility. Pregnancy after fibroid treatment requires close monitoring. Emerging therapies require further long-term safety data.

content: A frequent misconception is that all fibroids cause symptoms—many are silent and harmless. Another is that fibroids always necessitate hysterectomy; however, uterus-sparing options exist. Some believe that fibroids lead inevitably to cancer, which is incorrect as fibroids are benign and rarely transform. Exercise and diet alone cannot cure fibroids, but a healthy lifestyle may reduce risk.

chunk_title: Psychosocial Impact and Quality of Life
content: Fibroids can significantly affect quality of life through chronic pain, heavy bleeding leading to anemia and fatigue, and reproductive challenges, which may cause emotional distress, anxiety, and depression. Social and occupational aspects may be impacted due to pain or menstrual interference. Awareness and supportive care addressing psychosocial needs are important components of fibroid management.
